current_example.problem:
Consider the region bounded by the curve $x=\sqrt{y},$ the vertical line $x=2,$ and the horizontal line $y=4,$ as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the line $x=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/a56f30e5912629c9854e68d4837a37dae55a005e98ef6cf5379b5eb81022afb7.png)
current_example.worked_solution:
We want to determine the limits of integration. To do so, we find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=2$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{y} & =2 \\ y & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=4$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/0748c87aa004f06f99a19ab4b7a2dadcf2f86920b53d1edd7ff19aced1d76f04.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(2)-(\sqrt{y})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}{[2-\sqrt{y}]}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}(4-4\sqrt{y}+y)\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {[4y-\frac{8}{3}{y}^{3/2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\pi [(4(4)-\frac{8}{3}(4)^{3/2}+\frac{(4)^{2}}{2})-(0)] \\  & =\pi [16-\frac{64}{3}+8] \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
